title: AI at the Edge, Built on Red Hat OpenShift, Supermicro, and Portworx
summary: Run AI inference at distributed edge sites on a compact two-node Red Hat OpenShift topology with resilient Portworx storage and fleet-wide management.
body_markdown:
### Summary


Red Hat OpenShift, Portworx by Everpure, and Supermicro provide a co-engineered foundation for running AI inference, containers, and virtual machines at distributed edge sites—with resilient local data services, data protection, and centralized fleet management.


AI inference is expanding beyond centralized data centers.


Computer vision on a factory floor, loss prevention and shelf analytics in stores, and real-time telemetry at cell sites can all benefit from processing data close to where it is generated. In the[2025 Data on Kubernetes survey](https://dok.community/data-on-kubernetes-report-2025/) of 182 technology professionals, 61% said edge computing was essential to their data strategy, while 64% cited real-time data processing as critical to AI success.


But there is a gap between identifying a valuable edge AI use case and operating it reliably across hundreds or thousands of locations.


Red Hat,[Portworx® by Everpure](https://www.everpuredata.com/products/kubernetes-data-management.html) , and Supermicro are helping close that gap. Red Hat OpenShift two-node with arbiter provides a compact Kubernetes topology for distributed sites. Portworx adds a resilient, software-defined data layer. A validated Supermicro appliance brings the components together in a preconfigured deployment path for AI inference, containers, and virtual machines at the edge.


## **When AI inference belongs at the edge**


Running inference locally is not the right choice for every workload. It becomes compelling when one or more operating requirements outweigh the efficiency of centralized infrastructure:


- **Latency:** A vision system identifying a production defect or a queue forming at self-checkout may need to respond faster than a Wide Area Network (WAN) round trip permits.
- **Bandwidth:** Sending raw video and sensor streams from every site can be expensive and unnecessary. Local processing can reduce upstream traffic to events, insights, or selected records.
- **Operational continuity:** Local inference can reduce dependence on WAN connectivity, allowing critical site functions to continue during an upstream outage.
- **Data locality:** Privacy, sovereignty, contractual, or regulatory requirements may restrict how data is transferred or retained. Processing data near its source can help organizations meet those requirements.


These benefits come with tradeoffs. Edge sites have limited power, cooling, accelerator capacity, and on-site expertise. Platform teams must also distribute models, protect application data, monitor the fleet, and keep software consistent across locations. The right architecture starts with the workload and its service-level requirements, not with an assumption that every inference service belongs at the edge.


## **The edge dilemma: Availability versus cost**


[Portworx Edge](https://portworx.com/solutions/edge-data-management/) is designed for small Kubernetes deployments of up to five nodes, including retail stores, manufacturing lines, remote facilities, and network-edge sites.


For mission-critical locations, a node failure should not turn into a prolonged site outage. Conventional compact control plane and distributed storage designs have often used three full-sized nodes to establish quorum and tolerate a failure. Repeating that footprint across a large fleet increases hardware, licensing, power, and support costs.


Many small sites also lack the space, staff, or budget for a dedicated storage array. They may have intermittent connectivity and often have no dedicated storage administrator on site. The challenge is not simply making one cluster work. It’s creating a repeatable design that can be operated consistently across the fleet.


## **Two-node OpenShift with arbiter: Co-engineered for the edge**


Red Hat made two-node OpenShift with arbiter generally available with OpenShift 4.20. In November 2025, Red Hat and Portworx announced a[co-engineered design](https://www.redhat.com/en/blog/efficient-two-node-edge-infrastructure-red-hat-openshift-and-portworxpure-storage) combining this OpenShift topology with[Portworx Enterprise](https://portworx.com/products/portworx-enterprise/) .


Despite its name, the topology uses three machines:


- Two full control plane nodes run the OpenShift control plane, application workloads, virtual machines, and Portworx storage.
- A third, lightweight arbiter stores OpenShift etcd and Portworx KVDB state to maintain quorum. It does not run user workloads or hold application volume replicas.


Portworx can use replication factor 2 to synchronously replicate a volume across the two storage nodes. If one storage node fails, the volume retains a surviving replica, while the remaining data node and arbiter retain control plane and storage quorum.


This design tolerates one member failure, but infrastructure quorum is only part of application availability. Workload recovery time and performance depend on application behavior, storage policy, failure detection, and sufficient compute and accelerator capacity on the surviving node. Red Hat recommends planning each data node at no more than 50% utilization when the surviving node must absorb the full workload without performance degradation.


The combined architecture provides:


- Resilient persistent storage for containerized applications and OpenShift Virtualization VMs without a dedicated SAN or external storage array.
- Kubernetes-native provisioning, self-service storage, monitoring, and policy-driven capacity management.
- Namespace- and resource-selective data protection, with file- or folder-level recovery for supported OpenShift Virtualization environments and product versions.
- Centralized fleet management and observability through Red Hat Advanced Cluster Management, with optional Portworx monitoring and telemetry for the storage layer.


Deployment requirements have evolved since the initial announcement. The[current Portworx installation guide](https://docs.portworx.com/portworx-enterprise/platform/install/bare-metal/openshift-two-node-arbiter) requires Portworx Enterprise 3.5.2 or later, Portworx Operator 25.6.0 or later, OpenShift 4.20.11 or later, and PX-StoreV2. The arbiter must meet both Red Hat and Portworx requirements, including at least four physical CPU cores for Portworx. Consult the live documentation and Operator release notes for the recommended versions before deployment.


## **The stateful services around edge AI**


An inference endpoint can expose a stateless API, but the production system around it often depends on stateful data services.


### **Model artifacts**


A serving replica must obtain and load its model before it can process requests. Repeatedly downloading multi-gigabyte models over a constrained WAN can extend cold starts, node recovery, and scale-out time.


Model weights can come from object storage, a model repository, a persistent volume, an OCI artifact, or another supported source. Keeping an approved model on durable or cached site-local storage can reduce WAN re-fetching after a restart. The performance benefit must be tested with the selected serving runtime, model size, storage path, and accelerator configuration.


Storage activity is concentrated at startup for many LLM serving architectures. After the model has loaded into accelerator memory, the serving process normally does not read the weights continuously from disk.


### **RAG and local application data**


[Retrieval-augmented generation](https://www.everpuredata.com/knowledge/what-is-retrieval-augmented-generation.html) systems commonly depend on documents, metadata,[object storage](https://www.everpuredata.com/knowledge/what-is-object-storage.html) , and vector indexes. Edge applications may also use local inventory, telemetry, maintenance records, or site-specific operating data as context.


When those services must remain available during WAN disruption, they need a deliberate local persistence and protection strategy. Not every RAG system requires a complete vector database at every site; the placement depends on data ownership, update frequency, consistency, capacity, and recovery requirements.


### **Pipeline and operational state**


AI applications rarely consist of a model server alone. Sensor data, images, events, checkpoints, queues, databases, and workflow state may all participate in the pipeline. Protecting those services can be more important to continuity than protecting a replaceable inference pod.


Without a durable or reachable copy of required data, a node failure can force the application to redownload a model, rebuild an index, replay a pipeline, or wait for WAN access. That can significantly extend recovery at a site with limited hands-on support.


### **KV cache and session state**


LLM serving engines normally maintain the KV cache in GPU or host memory. Some architectures can share or offload completed cache blocks to CPU memory, a filesystem, or object storage, but this is an optional optimization with latency, capacity, and complexity tradeoffs.


[KV cache](https://blog.everpuredata.com/purely-technical/cut-llm-inference-costs-with-kv-caching/) should not be confused with durable application session state. Teams should evaluate cache offload only when prefix reuse, long-context serving, prefill/decode disaggregation, or memory pressure makes it valuable. Persistent user, workflow, or transaction state should be designed and protected separately.


## **A validated edge AI appliance from Supermicro, Red Hat, and Portworx**


In July, Supermicro[announced the launch](https://www.supermicro.com/en/pressreleases/supermicro-simplifies-edge-ai-deployments-validated-kubernetes-appliances-red-hat) of validated Kubernetes Edge AI appliances developed with Red Hat and Portworx by Everpure.


The documented architecture combines two Supermicro data nodes with a separate lightweight arbiter. Red Hat OpenShift provides the common application platform, while Portworx aggregates local storage into a synchronously replicated data layer. The preloaded hardware and software are available through Supermicro.


The appliance is intended for distributed sites running AI inference, containers, and virtual machines. Supermicro offers multiple data node configurations, with GPU options in selected medium and large tiers. Customers should size the configuration for their models and workloads and confirm subscriptions, services, support responsibilities, availability, power, cooling, and networking requirements before deployment.


As Red Hat’s Kelly Switt said in the announcement, “Red Hat OpenShift delivers that foundation, providing the common hybrid cloud application environment that simplifies the complexity of deploying, orchestrating, and managing AI workloads.” Portworx extends that foundation with persistent storage, replication, and data management designed to operate inside the Kubernetes cluster at each site.


## **Getting started**


Start with one site profile and one use case where latency, bandwidth, data locality, or continuity makes local inference valuable. Then validate the complete application rather than only the model server:


- Measure model distribution and cold-start time using the intended WAN and local storage paths.
- Confirm that the surviving node has enough compute, memory, storage performance, and accelerator capacity to run the required workload.
- Test a data-node failure and measure storage behavior, application recovery time, and performance after rescheduling.
- Disconnect the WAN and verify which functions continue, which data remains available, and how the site reconciles when connectivity returns.
- Test backup and restore for the databases, indexes, configurations, and other persistent services the application depends on.
- Validate how model updates, platform patches, observability, and security policies will be applied across the fleet.


AI at the edge works best when compute placement and data placement are designed together. Red Hat OpenShift, Portworx, and Supermicro provide a validated foundation for that design—one that combines a compact footprint with resilient local data services and centralized operations.


Read the[Portworx two-node arbiter installation guide](https://docs.portworx.com/portworx-enterprise/platform/install/bare-metal/openshift-two-node-arbiter) , explore[Portworx for Red Hat OpenShift](https://portworx.com/red-hat-openshift/) , or learn more about the[Supermicro validated solution](https://www.supermicro.com/solutions/Solution_Brief_Portworx_by_Everpure_Red_Hat_OpenShift.pdf) .
